title: xout - rules your coding agent actually follows
description: Cross out the coding-agent behavior you never want again. xout turns what's left into rules and plugs them into Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Copilot, pi, Kiro, or any tool that reads AGENTS.md.
social_image_alt: The agent behavior “Should I start?” is crossed out in red while “Fixed. Tests pass.” compiles into “Act first. Report after.”
hero_title: Cross out the agent behavior you never want again.
hero_body: Every AI coding tool follows a rules file, and almost nobody writes a good one. xout shows you two concrete things your agent could do - in a bugfix, a new feature, and a risky migration - and you cross out the one you never want to see again. xout writes the rules and plugs them into the tool you use: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Copilot, pi, Kiro, or anything that reads AGENTS.md.
proof_line: 15 cross-outs · three scenes (two routine, one hard to reverse) · every one of the eight axes backed by your X's · one line to enable, one to roll back
first_screen_notice: Run the session in English with --lang en (Japanese and Chinese: --lang ja / zh, shipping in the next release). Without the flag it runs in Korean. The event ledger doesn't care which language you used.
trust_dependencies: no third-party Python packages at runtime
demo_summary: Watch a real terminal session: 15 X's, 8 rules (0.6 MB GIF)
demo_alt: A real xout terminal session: fifteen cross-outs, eight compiled rules, applied with one keystroke.
storyboard_accessible: Story: the input is “Fix the bug.” Two behaviors appear. “Should I start?” is crossed out; “Fixed. Tests pass.” is kept, no approval needed. xout writes the rule “Act first on reversible changes; confirm first on irreversible ones.” The next response is “Fixed. Tests pass. Here is what changed.”
storyboard_followup: The storyboard above is the whole example; the animation is just decoration.
story_rule: Act first on reversible changes; confirm first on irreversible ones.
story_next: Fixed. Tests pass. Here is what changed.
mechanism_title: One red line removes a behavior. What's left becomes an instruction.
mechanism_intro: Two concrete responses to the same coding task. Cross out the one you never want to see again.
how_it_works_alt: Animation: a circle of 6,561 possible agents is cut in half eight times, one axis per cut, until the thinnest slice is left; it becomes eight rules plugged into your tool's rules file.
how_it_works_caption: Every X cuts what's left in half and drops the half you never want. Eight cuts, eight rules, plugged into your tool.
left_transcript: Before fixing pagination, asks whether tests and cleanup are in scope.
right_transcript: Fixes pagination, runs the relevant tests, then reports what changed along with the evidence.
rail_caption: The counter shows how many candidates are left. XOUT.md and manifest.json hold the behavior you actually chose and the evidence for it, and `xout why` traces every rule back to your X's.
rule_text: Write a short plan first, then proceed immediately. However, for hard-to-reverse work like deletes, pushes, deploys, and migrations, always get approval before executing.
outcome_title: Turn the thing your agent keeps doing into a rule.
outcome_intro: Make the same request before and after enabling xout. The compiled rule tells your agent's next session how to behave.
outcome_after: Fixed. Tests pass. Here is what changed.
outcome_xout: Rules, plugged into each tool's own rules file with one owned line or block.
outcome_manifest: The evidence and source behind every rule.
outcome_settings: A proposal for you to review; nothing turns on until you enable it.
outcome_activation: Enable with one line; roll back by removing that one line.
outcome_axes: Eight strike-backed axes: autonomy, scope, test discipline, comments and docs, error handling, commit policy, verification before done, and dependency policy. Five are measured in both routine and hard-to-reverse scenes; when your X's differ between the two, the rule is compiled with that condition attached.
start_title: Run your first pair on your own machine.
quickstart_body: One command in your terminal. Or run the session as a conversation: inside Claude Code, /xout:xout shows each pair in chat and records only the choice you make.
quickstart_note: Finish 15 cross-outs, apply with one keystroke, then repeat the request that used to annoy you in a fresh session of your agent. `xout why` shows the receipts, `xout probe` checks that the rules hold, `xout undo` takes everything back.
plugin_install_summary: Install as a checksum-verified Claude Code plugin
step_one_body: Download the plugin ZIP, SHA256SUMS, and the verifier together. Check the checksums first, then extract into a fresh versioned directory.
step_two_body: Install the extracted package from your local marketplace.
step_three_body: Run the session as a conversation: the agent shows each pair in chat, you pick the one to X, and it records only that choice. Then enable the import and check the status.
boundaries_title: Useful because you know exactly where it stops.
boundary_local_body: Your files, your install, your decision to turn it on.
boundary_runtime_title: No LLM calls, no network, no telemetry
boundary_runtime_body: The whole session runs in your terminal. It makes no model calls and no remote requests, and leaves no analytics trail.
boundary_replay_title: Append-only, replays the same every time
boundary_replay_body: Your X's are recorded in order and always replay to the same result.
boundary_activation_title: Turning it on and off is explicit
boundary_activation_body: Enable it when you're ready. Rolling back removes only the one line xout added.
boundary_recheck_body: After a week, look at whether the rules still fit. A rule that survived was never crossed out; that isn't the same as being right.
share_title: One sentence, with the README behind it.
share_sentence: You cross out the behavior you never want again; xout turns what's left into a rule on your machine.
footer_note: Rules for your coding agent that you can read, trace, and keep on your own machine.
